name: OpenJDK HotSpot (Java): xemantic/java-2-times-faster-than-c node-ring mutation benchmark
baseline: C (gcc -O3, java_2_times_faster_than_c.c: malloc/free for every node and every payload)
workload: Build a ring of 10,000 doubly linked nodes with variable-size byte payloads (0-49 bytes), then run 1,000,000 mutations that each delete and insert up to 200 nodes at pseudo-random (sin/fmod based) counts, ending with a checksum.
claimed_speedup: Java 8.569 s vs C 12.800 s (gcc script) and 12.726 s (clang-labelled script, actually gcc): about 1.49x faster (derived from page data). The project title says 'almost 2 times', but its own numbers show about 1.5x. Rust 13.8 s, Go 14.5 s, Node 26.2 s and C# 34.0 s in the same README are not faster than C.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc -O3 ... -lm (build-gcc.sh; compiler version not stated). build-clang.sh is labelled clang but also invokes gcc -O3, so both C rows are gcc. Java: java -cp build/classes/java/main with no JVM flags; JVM version not stated (README mentions Java 15).
hardware: Intel Core i7-8550U @ 1.80GHz (4 cores, 8 threads), 16 GB RAM (cpuinfo shown in README)
why_faster: Stated by the author: certain allocation-heavy algorithms gain performance from automatic memory management (no explicit free, generational allocation) and HotSpot's profile-driven inlining; the README says the exact cause is a hypothesis.
tradeoffs: JVM startup, warm-up and GC threads are inside the wall-clock (user time 8.7 s vs real 8.6 s); no memory figures are reported; needs a JVM.
caveats: The author admits the title is provocative and that a C version with a custom or pooled allocator beats Java (issue #1, not reproduced in the README); the C code calls malloc twice per node and free twice per delete, so this measures malloc/free against a generational GC for one allocation pattern, not C against Java in general. Single 'time' run per binary on a laptop (no variance, turbo/thermal effects), gcc version unstated, repo last touched in 2021 (JDK 15 era).
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/language-comparison, which lists 'xemantic/java-2-times-faster-than-c: Experiment showing JVM code running about twice as fast as equivalent native C'

name: OpenJDK HotSpot (Java): xemantic/java-2-times-faster-than-c almost_pseudo_random (sin and fmod loop)
baseline: C (gcc -O3, almost_pseudo_random.c using libm sin() and fmod())
workload: 1,000,000,000 iterations summing fmod(sin(i * 100000.0) + 1.0, 1.0), printing the checksum.
claimed_speedup: Java 51.235 s vs C 64.433 s (gcc script) and 64.878 s (clang-labelled script, actually gcc): about 1.26x faster (derived from page data). The README also reports Go at 28.191 s (about 2.3x faster than C, but with slightly different results) and Rust at 67.944 s.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc -O3 ... -lm (build-gcc.sh; compiler version not stated). build-clang.sh is labelled clang but also invokes gcc -O3, so both C rows are gcc. Java: java -cp build/classes/java/main with no JVM flags; JVM version not stated (README mentions Java 15).
hardware: Intel Core i7-8550U @ 1.80GHz (4 cores, 8 threads), 16 GB RAM (cpuinfo shown in README)
why_faster: Not established. The author offers three unverified hypotheses (HotSpot inlining, libm functions that cannot be inlined, a cheaper floating-point % in Java) and writes that the result is one he 'cannot explain'. Agent inference: HotSpot's own sin/drem intrinsics versus glibc sin range reduction on large arguments, so this is likely a math-library difference.
tradeoffs: JVM startup is negligible at 51 s; checksum text differs only by number formatting.
caveats: Dominated by the trigonometric library, not by compiler code generation; no mechanism is confirmed, so the tier is capped at C. The Go port computes sin differently and gets slightly different values. Single run on an i7-8550U laptop; C compiled without -ffast-math or -march=native; gcc version unstated; repo last updated 2021.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/language-comparison (same repo as the node-ring entry)

name: OpenJDK HotSpot (Java 25): benchLANG binary trees
baseline: C (GCC 16.2.0, malloc and free per node, 1.010 s) and C++ (GCC 16.2.0, new and delete per node, 1.147 s)
workload: CLBG-style binary trees with depths 4 to 18: a stretch tree, a long-lived tree, then many short-lived trees built, checked and (in C/C++) freed, one allocation per node.
claimed_speedup: Java 0.347 s vs C 1.010 s and C++ 1.147 s: about 2.9x faster than C and 3.3x faster than C++ (derived from page data). Peak RSS 987.8 MiB for Java vs 33.3 MiB for C and 35.4 MiB for C++.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off -s (GCC 16.2.0); C++: g++ -std=c++20 with the same flags. Java: OpenJDK 25.0.4, javac bench.java then java bench with default heap and default GC.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz (performance governor), 48 GB DDR4-3600 CL16, Arch Linux with i3-wm; results dated 3 September 2026, one run per language
why_faster: Stated by the suite's methodology: 'Binary trees: ... Allocator + GC + pointer chase, native code frees inside the timer, GC runtimes collect when they like'. Agent inference: per-node malloc/free (C, C++) against bump-pointer allocation and deferred or concurrent collection in a managed runtime; the C/C++ programs do not use an arena.
tradeoffs: About 30x the peak memory of C; whole-process CPU time exceeds wall time because of GC and JIT threads; needs a JVM.
caveats: One run per language ('1 run/lang'), no variance. In-program wall times: JIT warm-up is inside the managed runtimes' timed region, but their garbage collection can run partly outside it ('GC runtimes collect when they like'). An arena or pool allocator in C/C++ would likely beat every managed runtime here (compare the Arena variant in LangArena). Only the binary-trees column is a managed-runtime win: on primes, fib, strings and mandelbrot the managed runtimes lose to C or tie with it. The README header says 'Updated May 2026' but the table is dated 3 September 2026. The Java run uses the default collector and default heap sizing on a 48 GB machine, so part of the garbage may never be collected inside the timed region (agent inference).
found_via: WebSearch (github.com): 'cross-language benchmark repo Java C# beats C++ Rust binary trees allocation GC faster results README same algorithm gcc -O3' surfaced GlebOlsen/benchLANG; README results table and bench.c/bench.java/bench.cpp read

workload: Allocate, sum and free a complete binary tree of individually allocated nodes, repeated per iteration (idiomatic object version of binary-trees).
claimed_speedup: TypeScript/Bun/JIT 0.973 s and JS/Bun/JIT 1.042 s vs C++/G++ 2.101 s (prod, -O2) and 2.098 s for the best of all 16 C/C++ configurations: about 2.2x and 2.0x faster (derived from page data). Peak RSS about 647 MB for Bun vs about 66 MB for C/Clang.
compiler_and_flags: C/C++: Clang 22.1.8 and GCC 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk). Headline 'prod' build is -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer; the same suite also builds 'Fast' (-O3 -march=native -funroll-loops, thin LTO), 'Unsafe' (-O3 -march=native -ffast-math, full LTO) and 'PGO' variants, and all 16 Clang/GCC x C/C++ configurations were compared here. Bun: results file lists TypeScript/Bun/JIT, TypeScript/Bun/Compiled and JS/Bun/JIT (Bun version in the results file).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78GB RAM, x86_64 Linux (results file 2026-10-05, host kostya-ms7c37)
why_faster: Not stated in prose. The suite's own Binarytrees::Arena control (index-based arena, same tree) reverses the result in C/C++, which points at per-node make_unique/malloc cost versus JavaScriptCore's bump allocation and generational GC (agent inference).

name: LuaJIT 2.0 FFI: dyu/ffi-overhead plusone() call loop
baseline: C and C++ (gcc 5.4.1 -O2) calling plusone() in the shared library libnewplus.so through the dynamic linker
workload: Call the C function plusone(int) in a loop 500,000,000 times (while (x < count) x = plusone(x)) and report elapsed milliseconds.
claimed_speedup: LuaJIT 891 ms and 905 ms vs C 1182 ms and 1182 ms (C++ 1182 and 1183 ms) for 500M calls: about 1.3x faster (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: C and C++: gcc/g++ 5.4.1 -O2 -fPIC (Tuprules.tup), executable linked against newplus/libnewplus.so; luajit 2.0.4; julia 0.6.3; Ubuntu 14.04; 2 samples per language.
hardware: Intel i7-3630QM laptop (4 cores, HT), 16 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Gain only applies to call-boundary overhead for very small functions.
caveats: Measures foreign-call overhead for a trivial function, not code quality. The C and C++ rows call through the PLT of a shared library, which the FFI/ccall code of the JIT languages avoids; statically linking or LTO-inlining plusone in C would remove the call entirely (agent inference from the Tupfile; the README itself states no mechanism, so the tier is capped at C; an HN search snippet reported a commenter attributing a LuaJIT-over-C result to direct calls versus PLT calls, but it did not name this repo). C is compiled -O2, not -O3. Toolchains are from 2018 (julia 0.6.3, luajit 2.0.4, gcc 5.4.1) and only 2 samples are shown. Many other languages in the table are slower than C (Go 37,975 ms, Node 9,163 ms, Java 4,469 ms).

name: NativeMinuit.jl (pure-Julia port of C++ Minuit2)
baseline: C++ Minuit2 (ROOT's standalone Minuit2 built through CMake, default Release, C++17) running MIGRAD on the same objectives
workload: Wall time of a full MIGRAD minimization with Strategy(0) on five test objectives: quad_4d, rosenbrock_2d, rosenbrock_10d, gauss_ll_10_1000, gauss_ll_2_100.
claimed_speedup: Julia/C++ time ratios 0.147x (quad_4d: 0.81 us vs 5.50 us), 0.253x (rosenbrock_2d: 9.50 vs 37.62 us), 0.371x (rosenbrock_10d: 58.11 vs 156.62 us), 0.718x (gauss_ll_10_1000: 32.26 vs 44.96 us), 0.888x (gauss_ll_2_100: 20.16 vs 22.71 us): about 1.1x to 6.8x faster (derived from page data). README: 'Faster than C++ Minuit2 on every benchmark in the test corpus'.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.12 with OpenBLAS 0.3.29, single-threaded BLAS on both sides; C++ side built with benchmark/cpp/CMakeLists.txt (CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE defaults to Release, C++17); C++ compiler and exact flags not stated.
why_faster: Stated by the README: a parametric CostFunction{F} devirtualizes the FCN call site at compile time, whereas C++ Minuit2 pays for shared_ptr ref-counting and ABObj expression-template dispatch.
stars_or_usage: 14 stars; registered in the Julia General registry
tradeoffs: Needs the Julia runtime and JIT warm-up (the README table does not say whether compile time is excluded); a derivative work of Minuit2, so LGPL applies; not a drop-in for C++ callers.
caveats: First-party numbers from the port's author, microsecond-scale runs on toy objectives of 2 to 10 parameters where call and dispatch overhead dominate; the C++ compiler and flags are not stated, and the C++ Minuit2 tree the CMake file expects at reference/Minuit2_cpp is not in the repository listing, so the C++ version is unspecified. The port reimplements the algorithm; the README says its algorithms were 'audited against C++ Minuit2', but the page shows no equal iteration or function-call counts. The stated mechanism (call-site devirtualization) suggests the gain is dispatch and inlining of the user function rather than the numerical core.

name: Julia vs C++11 random-walk Monte Carlo (jlapeyre/ranwalk-Julia-vs-Cxx)
baseline: C++11 std::mt19937 with std::bernoulli_distribution(0.5), compiled with c++ -std=c++11 -O3 (Debian gcc 4.9.1)
workload: 100,000 random walks of 3,000 coin flips each, accumulating a histogram of final displacements.
claimed_speedup: C++-11 3.88 s vs Julia v0.3 1.27 s and Julia v0.4 1.68 s: about 3.1x and 2.3x faster (derived from page data); the README says 'The Julia code runs three times faster than the C++ code'.
compiler_and_flags: c++ -std=c++11 -O3 (Debian 4.9.1-15 gcc 4.9.1; -march=native was slower); Julia 0.3.4-pre and 0.4
why_faster: Stated by the README: the time is almost all random number generation, and Julia's rand(Bool) is much faster than the GNU C++11 <random> bernoulli_distribution path; the author says this does not support 'Julia is faster than C++'.
tradeoffs: Toy benchmark; Julia versions 0.3 and 0.4 are obsolete (the 2024 commit only updated the scripts).
caveats: Not the same work: the C++ code draws a full Mersenne Twister output per coin flip through bernoulli_distribution, while Julia's rand(Bool) consumes random bits more cheaply, so this compares RNG front ends, not compilers (agent inference from rwtest_simple.cc and rwtest_simple.jl). The author notes a faster C++ program is possible. No licence file, so the code is reference only. gcc 4.9.1-era results, CPU model not stated, single timing per language.
